explanations.explanation: Six it is, friend. Ezekiel sees six men coming from the Upper Gate, which faces north, and each one has a weapon of slaughter in his hand (Ezekiel 9:2). Ezekiel the priest counted them, and that's a good habit when something this heavy walks in. This is a serious scene, so I'm keeping my apron straight.

Close, but the text says six, not four. Ezekiel sees six men coming from the Upper Gate, each with a weapon of slaughter in his hand (Ezekiel 9:2). Four is a nice round number, I'll give you that. It's just not the one in the verse.

Twelve would be a whole crowd, friend, but the text says six. Ezekiel sees six men coming from the Upper Gate, each with a weapon of slaughter in his hand (Ezekiel 9:2). I think twelve sounds right because it's a number that comes up a lot in the Bible. Here, it's six.

A writing kit, yes. The man clothed in linen has it at his side, and he walks in with the six men who carry weapons (Ezekiel 9:2). Six weapons and one writing kit. I'd be checking my pockets for a pen right about now.

A ram's horn would make some noise, but that's not what he carries. The man clothed in linen has a writing kit at his side (Ezekiel 9:2). Nobody in this verse blows a horn. This man came to write, not to sound an alarm.

No lamp here, friend. The man clothed in linen has a writing kit at his side (Ezekiel 9:2). I think a lamp is a fair guess for a man walking through a city, but the text gives him something to write with.

That's it. The LORD says to put a mark on the foreheads of the men "sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there" (Ezekiel 9:4). The mark goes on the ones who are grieved by what's happening in the city. I think that's one of the most tender details in a very heavy passage.

explanations.answer: Those who bring offerings to the altar
explanations.explanation: The altar is in the scene, since the men stand beside the bronze altar (Ezekiel 9:2), but the mark isn't about offerings. The LORD says it goes on the foreheads of the men "sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there" (Ezekiel 9:4). The text names what they're doing, which is groaning. That's the whole description.

explanations.answer: Those who live closest to the temple
explanations.explanation: Where a man lives doesn't decide it, friend. The LORD says the mark goes on the men "sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there" (Ezekiel 9:4). Closeness to the temple isn't in the verse. Being grieved over what's going on is.

This one is the opposite, friend. The LORD says, "do not show pity or spare anyone!" (Ezekiel 9:5). Nothing in the verse says pity gets offered to someone who begs. It's a hard line to read, and I won't dress it up.

False is right. The LORD tells the six, "do not show pity or spare anyone!" (Ezekiel 9:5). Nothing in that verse mentions anyone begging, and no pity is allowed. It's a heavy line, but it's what the text says.

Yes, that's the exception. The LORD says, "do not go near anyone who has the mark" (Ezekiel 9:6). That's why the man in linen went first with his writing kit. The mark settles who the six don't touch.

The altar is where the seven men stood when they came in (Ezekiel 9:2), but it isn't the line God draws. He says the six must not go near anyone who has the mark (Ezekiel 9:6). Standing at the altar isn't mentioned there.
Running isn't what protects anyone here, friend. The six are told not to go near anyone who has the mark (Ezekiel 9:6). The text says nothing about people running. The mark is the thing that matters.

Sanctuary, right. God says, "Now begin at My sanctuary," and they begin with the elders who were before the temple (Ezekiel 9:6). It's a hard place to start, and the text doesn't give us God's reason. I think that's worth a quiet moment.
A palace isn't mentioned in this verse. God says, "Now begin at My sanctuary" (Ezekiel 9:6). The word "My" is right there. The sanctuary is His, and that's where it starts.
Borders would mean starting at the outside and working in. God says the opposite: "Now begin at My sanctuary" (Ezekiel 9:6). The elders who were before the temple are the first ones the six come to.

explanations.answer: If He will destroy everyone left in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's his question. Ezekiel falls facedown and cries out, "Oh, Lord GOD, when You pour out Your wrath on Jerusalem, will You destroy the entire remnant of Israel?" (Ezekiel 9:8). He's left alone while the killing goes on. I think you can hear how heavy that is in his voice.

explanations.answer: Why He brought him to see Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Ezekiel doesn't ask that, friend. He falls facedown and asks, "will You destroy the entire remnant of Israel?" (Ezekiel 9:8). His question is about the people who are left. I think his heart is with them.

explanations.answer: If he can go and warn the city first
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Ezekiel ask to warn anyone. He falls facedown and asks, "will You destroy the entire remnant of Israel?" (Ezekiel 9:8). His question is about what's left of Israel, not about getting to the city first.

Forsaken, yes. God says the people claim, "The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see" (Ezekiel 9:9). Those are their words, not His. The verse puts them right beside the bloodshed and perversity God names.

Cleansed doesn't fit here, friend. God says the people claim, "The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see" (Ezekiel 9:9). It's a complaint, and God quotes it back. Cleansing isn't what they're saying.

Healed would be a happy thing to say about a land, but that's not the quote. God says the people claim, "The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see" (Ezekiel 9:9). They're saying the LORD has left and isn't looking.
Their deeds, right. God says, "I will bring their deeds down upon their own heads" (Ezekiel 9:10). The word "own" is in the verse. What comes back on them is what they did.

Idols were in the vision, since God showed Ezekiel idols at the temple earlier (Ezekiel 8:3-16), but that's not what this verse says. God says, "I will bring their deeds down upon their own heads" (Ezekiel 9:10). It's their deeds that come down.
A famine isn't named in this verse. God says, "I will bring their deeds down upon their own heads" (Ezekiel 9:10). I'd stay with the words He actually gives. The word is deeds.

True. The man clothed in linen with the writing kit at his side reports back, "I have done as You commanded" (Ezekiel 9:11). That's the last line of the passage, and it's short and plain. He was sent to do something and he reports that it's done.

It's actually true, friend. The man clothed in linen with the writing kit at his side reports back, "I have done as You commanded" (Ezekiel 9:11). It's a short report and the passage ends right there. Nothing in the verse says he held anything back.
